records.title: Pension systems revisited in the age of automation and an aging economy
Measuring Water Content in Hydroponic Plants Based on PH Values and Nutriens Using Fuzzy Logic Microcontroller Based Tsukamoto
records.venue: Journal Of Computer Networks Architecture and High Performance Computing
records.abstract: Hydroponic cultivation is a method of planting without soil by utilizing water containing nutrients and oxygen at certain levels. Regulation and monitoring of pH, nutrients (TDS), and water temperature are crucial factors in the success of a hydroponic system. Inaccuracies in nutrient water management can significantly affect plant growth. This study aims to design an automation system capable of monitoring pH and water nutrient levels using the Fuzzy Tsukamoto method based on the Nodemcu ESP32 microcontroller. The sensors used in this study are the MSP340 pH Module sensor to measure acidity (pH) and the Df Robot Module TDS sensor to detect nutrient levels in water. The Fuzzy Tsukamoto method is applied to make fuzzy logic-based decision-making, where the input values of pH and nutrients are converted into linguistic variables. The fuzzyfication process is carried out to determine the level of plant fertility, while the inference method is used to produce output based on previously set rules. This monitoring system also utilizes the Nutrient Film Technique (NFT) technique with a linear regression method to optimize the use of water pumps, making it more energy efficient. With the design of this system, hydroponic farmers can monitor water conditions automatically and in real-time, increasing efficiency and reducing human error in nutrient water management. The results of this study are expected to provide innovative solutions for the development of more efficient and sustainable hydroponic systems.

records.title: Old‐Age Support Policy Effects on Economic Growth and Fertility
records.abstract: ABSTRACT Salient features of major economies around the world, specifically in high‐income countries, are graying population and declining fertility. Incorporating the quantity–quality tradeoff of children into an overlapping generations model, this paper presents an analysis of the effects of formal old‐age support on fertility and economic growth. Because of health risks during old age, which might be too severe to be covered privately, some economically developed countries have public old‐age support programs. Formal old‐age support provision is regarded as involving management costs, for instance, caused by X‐inefficiency in addition to labor costs. Findings demonstrate that when management costs are sufficiently small, formal old‐age support raises the balanced economic growth rate, involving a smaller tax burden and freeing individual time from family old‐age support, but it lowers fertility. Effects on the lifetime utility of individuals are indeterminate. By contrast, when management costs are high, the increased formal old‐age support deters economic growth through a negative income effect. However, it also lowers the fertility rate. In this case, lifetime utility becomes lower. Our major finding is that, when the cost inefficiency of public support is not high, formal old‐age support might increase long‐term lifetime welfare of individuals, but it lowers fertility.

records.title: Polygamy and educational attainment of children in a rural community in Rivers State, Nigeria
records.venue: Journal of Health Applied Sciences and Management
records.abstract: This study examined polygamy and educational attainment of children in Khana Local Government Area of Rivers State, Nigeria. The objective of the study was to explain the relationship between polygamy and educational attainment of children. The study made use of descriptive research design. A structured questionnaire was used to raise data for the study with a reliability index of 0.98. A sample size of 500 respondents was used which was determined through purposive sampling technique. Data were presented in frequency distribution tables and analyzed through the aid of percentage and Pearson Product Moment correlation coefficient set at 0.05 level of significance. The study disclosed that there existed a significant relationship between polygamy and educational attainment of children in Khana Local Government Area of Rivers State, Nigeria. The causes were inadequate funding of children’s education by their families and the challenges of unfriendly environment they were faced with at their homes which were not supportive to their educational pursuit. The outcomes were poor academic performance and school dropout, among others. The study recommended that only men with the right financial ability should practice polygamy. The study also stated that family planning should be practiced by polygamous families in order to have family size that can be well handled in terms of children’s education.

records.title: Review of periodical literature for 2023: (iv) 1700–1850
records.abstract: The topic of industrial revolution and industrial development attracted particular attention in 2023. Using econometric analysis Kelly et al. analysed growth pattern across English counties between 1760s and 1830s using male employment patterns to compare the contrasting explanations of the industrial revolution. They focused on textiles and iron industries and found that mechanical and related skills were crucial. Overall, Kelly et al. found that industrialization occurred in areas with low wages and high mechanical skills, whereas factors such as literacy, banks, and proximity to coal had little explanatory power. The work of Otojanov et al. on the other hand supported the ‘induced innovation’ hypothesis as the driving force of the industrial revolution, as cheap energy and capital induced adoption of labour-saving technologies. However, they also found that until the 1820s labour saving was modest. Galofré-Vilà explored the role of informal networks in spurring innovative activity. The author found that counties with a large number of informal networks such as Freemasonry, friendly societies, libraries, and booksellers were more innovative and produced more patents and exhibits for the 1851 Crystal Palace World's Fair. Several articles focused on industrial development. Sugden et al. explored the role of geographical factors, especially proximity to coal, for the location of woollens industry in the West Riding. They found that the key factors that facilitated the concentration in this region were coal, low cost of living, and running water. Allen studied the coal industry and transport. He found that coal markets were highly integrated, and productivity of coal shipments grew between 1695 and 1824, while the geographical pattern of production remained practically the same. Allen found that among the main reasons for the unchanging geographical pattern was the power of the Northeast coal producers that blocked the building of midland canals that would open up the market. Raman explored the role of the spinner's skill and dexterity for determining the final quality of cotton cloth. She argued that the trajectory of the British cotton industry was shaped by the pursuit of matching the quality of Indian cotton textiles and, unable to match the skills of the Indian artisans, British entrepreneurs turned to mechanization. Research on labour and living standards was also strongly represented. Sheng explored the limitations of the method of inferring time-use from court testimony. The author used Old Bailey records to study women's working time in London in 1750–1830. Sheng found that, unlike previous research that concluded that men worked longer in paid employment, women in his sample spent only slightly more time in paid work in the 1830s than in the 1750s. Sheng further argued that another limitation of the simulated time-use recall method for generating aggregate data on times worked in paid work also lies in the fact that sectoral distribution of subjects in the dataset may be biased. Paker et al. explored hiring and employment histories of over 1000 labourers employed in the rebuilding of St Paul's Cathedral between 1672 and 1748. They found that over the studied period the hiring strategies shifted towards labour retention and giving priority to core labourers. In this way, the employment strategies at the Cathedral were in stark contrast to the volatility that characterized pre-industrial labour demand. They also found that day wage rates remained flat over the period, but core workers had access to higher earnings, as they were given more days to work through retention and rehiring, and access to more lucrative watchman shifts. Several articles explored living standards and poor relief. Horrell relied on expenditure patterns of ordinary households between 1260 and 1869 to construct a chained-Laspeyres price index. The author used estimates of consumption of food; articles such as fuel and candles, clothing, etc.; housing costs; and durables such as furniture to reconstruct family expenditures in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Horrell’s work shows a switch away from dairy with industrialization, the responsiveness of meat and poultry consumption to economic conditions, and the shift from beer consumption to beverages such as tea from the mid-eighteenth century. The author argued that, although the results are similar to ‘bare bones’ and the ‘respectability basket’, until the eighteenth century the chained-Laspeyres price index is superior in capturing price levels over industrialization. This is because the shift towards spending on imported groceries and manufactured goods introduced a new dynamic that the chained-Laspeyres price index better captures. Bujokova and Desportes explored Scottish poor relief. They presented two case studies of poor relief in Scotland – Lowland and Highland – between c.1720 and 1790. They showed that towards the end of the eighteenth century the system of poor relief transitioned from one based on a community approach rooted in parish and kirk structures to one based on legalism and the concept of rights based social provision. They also highlighted the role of Scottish political economists’ ideas emphasizing progress and economic growth for this shift. Melander and Miotto examined the 1834 New Poor Law reform and its relationship to criminality. They found that the cut to welfare provision imposed by the reform led to increases in criminal activity with a 17.2 per cent increase in non-violent crime as compared with pre-reform yearly levels. Building a dataset of over 250 000 individual criminal charges between 1828 and 1840, they found that welfare cuts were related to a rise in non-violent property crimes, and these crimes occurred more in times of seasonal unemployment. Broadberry et al. presented a new chronology of business cycles for the period 1700–2010. They found that eighteenth-century business cycles had a shorter duration of 3.4 years and amplitude of 3.2 per cent than those in the post-1945 period, which were on average 16 years with an amplitude of 51.9 per cent. They found that the leading cause of economic fluctuations in the eighteenth century were shocks to agricultural production. The most important of these shocks was the Great Frost of 1709–10, which reduced GDP by 20 per cent. Eighteenth-century recessions were also caused by wars and financial crises. In the nineteenth century the importance of sectoral shocks, such as agricultural shocks, somewhat declined, whilst financial crises continued to be an important factor. The importance of wars declined only after the major economic shock brought by the Napoleonic wars. In the nineteenth century, increasing trade and capital liberalization saw shocks to commodity prices and international trade emerge as causes of recessions. In financial history, the focus was on the Bank of England and also on insurance. O'Brien and Palma, using recalibrated financial data, found that the Bank of England, even though it was a private institution, fulfilled a public role over the eighteenth century, well before the emergence of the Bagehot doctrine. The authors argue that, by providing financial intermediation, the Bank contributed to the development of the fiscal-naval state. Importantly, the Bank provided the state with credit, particularly at times when private credit was unavailable. Yet, the Bank had autonomy from the state and was able to deny the provision of funds when such a step undermined its financial safety. Milevsky focused on eighteenth-century debates surrounding choice architecture – how to design investment options in a retirement plan – and on default options and auto-enrolment into insurance schemes. The author studied the case of Adam Smith, who joined the annuity scheme Scottish Ministers’ Widows’ Fund when he was elected professor at the University of Glasgow. Very strongly represented was research on slavery. Absell studied the effects of slave emancipation in the British Empire on the sugar industry in Brazil. The author found that emancipation and subsequent trade liberalization led to increased demand for Brazilian sugar. Brazil thus saw an expansion of exports and its share of the world sugar market grew. Mishler explored enslaved people's engagement with the legal system in cases of legal activism in the British Empire. Roberts used slave ship drug invoices to relate the slave trade and captivity and drugs. Schwarz studied attitudes of important members of the Royal family towards the slave trade and abolition. The author shows the high level of polarization within the national debate on the issue of abolition by emphasizing that even within the Royal family there was a distinct division of opinion, with the Duke of Clarence, later William IV, favouring the slave trade. Radburn studied firms that supplied gunpowder to the slave trade and the stimulus that the trade gave to the explosives industry in Britain. The author emphasized that, as merchants from Bristol and Liverpool supplanted London slave merchants, new powder works opened in the areas focused on satisfying the specific demands from slave trading. However, as Radburn pointed out, only about 12 per cent of the British production of gunpowder was exported to Africa, so although the African market was essential to the firms connected to slave traders in the provinces, this did not apply to the industry as a whole. These firms were highly specialized, and the quality of the product they made precluded, for example, supplying the British state, and so even after abolition the firms continued to supply African markets. Business history was represented by articles on profit, trade, trading, and merchant networks and also had strong links to slavery. O'Sullivan explored the notion and the understanding of profit in the eighteenth century. To do so, the author studied revolts of Cornish copper miners in the late eighteenth century. O'Sullivan underlined that these revolts were not driven by luddism but were instead a protest against stoppages in mining activity undertaken by the owners who sought to decrease the supply of copper in efforts to increase prices and expand their profits whilst threatening the livelihood of the miners. She concluded that profit needs to be studied in a broader framework and in association with power. Ruderman and van Waijenburg examined the Royal African Company's behaviour in its post-monopoly period using letters to slave ship captains between 1685 and 1706. They emphasized the Company's organizational flexibility epitomized in better safeguarding of ships, more efficient management of slave voyages, and better monitoring of agents in Africa whose opportunities for cheating expanded with the opening of the slave trade. Sweet focused on the economic and social history of a British trading family involved principally in the slave trade – the family of Ambrose Lace. The author argues that, unlike some other British families and corporations whose business activities implicated them in slavery, the Laces focused on slavery as their main enterprise. Sweet links Ambrose Lace with the Calabar massacre and retells the subterfuge that Lace and his firm used to dissuade suspicion and to uphold their business reputation. Buckles presented a case study of John Pinney, a Bristol merchant with a plantation in Nevis, and his social network. The author modified historical social network analysis to better accommodate change over time by incorporating a 2-year moving memory total. Buckles used the methodology to study the business network of Pinney, the experience of enslaved people connected to the network, and the role of Pinney's wife Jane in the commercial network. Research on the economic role of women and their experience in the labour market was very strongly represented. Shepard emphasized that distinction between ‘productive’ and ‘reproductive’ work is a concept that originated in the nineteenth century and would make little sense to early modern women, as care work was often a commercial endeavour. Phillips examined the ways London theatre companies dealt with temporary absences of actresses due to childbearing in the late eighteenth century. The author found that about 20 per cent of actresses under contract with Covent Garden gave birth in the season 1784–5. Phillips found that actresses in major theatres received 1 or 2 months of maternity leave from at least 1770 onwards, and a range of accommodations were available for pregnant actresses. Furthermore, theatre managers also adapted the day-to-day business such as premieres, rehearsals, etc., to accommodate for actresses’ absence. Wakelam argued that the increasing marriage rates and the declining rates of women incarcerated due to indebtedness over the eighteenth century imply that women's economic independence declined. This finding is in contrast to the scholarship that emphasized the continued economic agency of women after marriage. Brock studied the ways in which women shaped private trade of the East India Company. The author reviewed over 1300 petitions addressed to the Company by women between 1600 and 1757 focusing on the various relationships and roles women had. Brock found that about 15 per cent of the petitions sent by women related to private trade in which women were involved and emphasized that women in merchant families had a degree of autonomy and that a woman's credit and trust was often separate from her husband's. Whitehead explored the role letter writing performed in establishing the political authority of elite women and the ways in which letters were used to negotiate patronage. Bolissian used popular health texts to challenge the masculinization hypothesis and claims that women bodies after menopause were perceived by early modern medicine as becoming increasingly masculine. Several papers explored institutions from varied perspectives. Grajzl and Murrell studied caselaw development around land, inheritance, and families, and its impact on economic development. They found that developments in caselaw related to families and inheritance shaped real-income growth. The authors argue that changes in caselaw allowed for new ways of distributing family property and thus enabled new commercial activities to take place. Dimitruk argued that the Glorious Revolution of 1688 expanded access to estate bills to gentry families. Most of the estate bills focused on removing entails and restrictions on the sale of land. The author argued that these acts facilitated Smithian growth in land and credit markets. However, Dimitruk emphasized that passing individual acts was second best to a wholesale reform of the inheritance institutions, as it created opportunities for rent-seeking on the part of members of parliament (MPs) and brokers who prepared the bills for gentry families. Taylor studied tolls on grain – payments made by merchants to market owners for the privilege to sell the grain on their market. The author found that over the eighteenth century tolls became increasingly criticized for obstructing trade, and some markets started to abolish the practice. Skjönsberg used the writings of a Quaker merchant Richard Champion to explore the role of ‘ordinary men’ in shaping eighteenth-century politics. Halliday emphasized English law's capacity for mutation. Lidwell-Durnin explored the role of scientific authority in dispelling public fear in the case of the 1782 London caterpillar outbreak – an invasion of brown-tail moth caterpillars, which prompted fears of famine and plague. Camoglu explored the experience of plague in 1722 London as depicted by Daniel Defoe in a novel A Journal of the Plague Year. The author emphasized the collectively shared experience of the disease against the physical experience of isolation that was an outcome of disease prevention protocols. Maritime history was represented by articles on risk and on institutional frameworks governing shipping. A series of papers on risk and uncertainty in the early modern world were published in the International Journal of Maritime History. Wade et al. argued for the need to reassess the ways that actors in the maritime economy dealt with risk and challenges brought by the natural environment as well as by political and social challenges. They show how this provides new insights into globalization and economic development in the early modern world. Reid explored risk mitigation strategies of British merchant ships and points towards small alterations in the construction of merchant ships that followed the specific demands of the shipyards’ clients connected to cargo capacity, structural integrity, and salaries of sailors. Reid thus empathized that sailing ship technologies remained static as previous research has argued but developed alongside the needs of its clients and with a view of natural hazards and commercial risks that sailing entailed. Dyble and Iodice introduced the AveTransRisk database that captures routes, cargo, weather conditions, ships, seafarers, and transaction costs of maritime trade. Jopling studied English privateering and challenged the perception that privateers believed in the notion of egalitarianism and had an anti-authority view. Instead, the author argued that, even though some elements of democracy were present, fragmentation between the notions of seventeenth-century buccaneers and privateers and eighteenth-century pirates existed, and this undermines the view that there was a universally shared ‘discipline’ observed by all. Tucker examined productivity of British shipping in the Atlantic using records of 25250 records of vessels entering and clearing Chesapeake Bay. The author found that over the eighteenth century port times decreased by about half and attributed this to increased attention to productivity, which was met by improved labour supply for ships. This labour supply was achieved through longer or more coercive contracts and thus decreased freedom for mariners. Articles on the history of economic thought focused on the Scottish Enlightenment and the political economy of population. Pye explored the writing of history in eighteenth-century Scotland and emphasized that, by rejecting the whiggish explanations of social progress and liberation brought by the Glorious Revolution, the Scottish Enlightenment brought focus on new explanations. The Scottish Enlightenment put a special stress on the role of commercial civilization and commerce as a force of modernization and a shift from the feudal past. records.title: Assessment of the perception, attitude, and practice of the local community to supplement the urban water system through rooftop rainwater harvesting in Addis Ababa
records.abstract: ABSTRACT Visual summary of rooftop rainwater harvesting in Addis Ababa. A mixed-methods study of 400 households shows RRWH supplies 45 L daily per household, meeting 4.47% of annual demand. Higher support exists among women, large families, and high-income groups. Key barriers include inadequate infrastructure and limited awareness. This study investigates community perceptions, attitudes, and practices regarding rooftop rainwater harvesting (RRWH) to supplement the urban water system of Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, a city facing significant water challenges. The research highlights the influence of demographic factors such as family size, gender, income level, and educational attainment on community acceptance of RRWH, the current supplemented amount and advances previous work in this area. The study employed a mixed-methods approach, utilizing a structured questionnaire for quantitative data collection from a stratified random sample of 400 households, and semistructured interviews for qualitative data. Findings indicated that larger families and females exhibit greater support for RRWH, while higher income and educational levels correlate with a preference for RRWH. Despite health concerns, a substantial portion of the community recognizes the acceptability of RRWH, suggesting strong potential for adoption. However, critical barriers, including inadequate infrastructure, insufficient governmental support, and a lack of awareness, hinder widespread implementation. The study estimated that RRWH could supplement approximately 45 litres per rainy day per household of the daily water demand of a household, emphasizing the importance of targeted educational campaigns and infrastructure investment to enhance RRWH adoption.

records.title: Assessment of Pregnancy Status in Patients with Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome and their Partners
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: HIV is a globally prevalent infection for which there is currently no cure or vaccine. As the number of individuals with HIV infection increases, so does the number of individuals wishing to have children despite being infected. This situation has highlighted issues related to couples where one partner is infected while the other is not (serodiscordant couples) and couples where both partners are positive. Major issues include pregnancy complications, transmission to the child, and potential side effects of the ART treatment on the health of the child. Women living with HIV who become pregnant or contract the virus during pregnancy are at risk for both maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality, especially if the virus is not adequately controlled. Additionally, there is a risk of vertical transmission through breastfeeding during pregnancy and postpartum. To mitigate the consequences of HIV during pregnancy, it is ideal to start with prepregnancy counseling and plan pregnancies during periods of minimal viral load using appropriate methods. AIMS AND OBJECTIVE: There are limited studies and shared experiences regarding fertility status and issues of HIV/AIDS patients, especially in Turkey. Hence, this study aimed to investigate the fertility status of HIV/AIDS patients and their partners followed up in our clinic, shed light on the encountered issues, and share our experiences. METHODS: This retrospective, observational, single-center cross-sectional study included HIV/AIDS patients and their partners followed at Hatay Mustafa Kemal University (MKÜ) Medical Faculty Hospital from January 2018 to December 2023. Demographic data of the patients, their sexual orientations, HIV/AIDS status of their partners and children, treatments received, CD4 cell counts, and viral load data were retrospectively obtained from the automation system of our hospital and patient files. RESULTS: Among the couples, there were 21 pairs where both partners were HIV positive, 10 pairs where the woman was HIV positive and the man was seronegative (serodiscordant), and 5 pairs where the man was HIV positive and the woman was seronegative. In our study, eight couples with both partners HIV positive had nine children, and six couples with women who were HIV positive (serodiscordant) had ten children. The five couples with men who were HIV positive (serodiscordant) had six children. No vertical transmission was observed in our study, but three patients did not attend regular follow-ups. During the follow-up period, no seroconversion was detected in the partners of serodiscordant patients. The average gestational age was 38 weeks, and the average birth weight was 2873 ± 349 grams. CONCLUSION: Our study found no vertical transmission and no seroconversion in partners of serodiscordant couples. Issues related to pregnancy in HIV-positive couples can be managed with pre-pregnancy counseling by specialists, protective methods, appropriate ART, and perinatal follow- up.

records.title: Socioeconomic Status of Workers in the Sugar Industry and Their Plight: The Case of the Northern Corridor, Cebu, Philippines
records.abstract: One significant issue in the Philippines today is widespread poverty, especially affecting individuals whose livelihoods depend on sugarcane. This problem is particularly pronounced in areas where large tracts of land, known as haciendas - a legacy of the Spanish land management system called encomienda - are owned by one or a few families. This study aimed to investigate the economic status of workers, known as tapaseros, in the sugarcane industry within the 4th District of Cebu, Philippines, to aid in the development of a proposed alternative livelihood program. This research employed a descriptive survey method, utilizing a researcher-designed questionnaire as the primary data collection tool to gather information on respondents’ profiles and economic conditions. The questionnaire underwent content validation by experts, and its reliability was confirmed with a Cronbach’s alpha value of 0.8121, indicating high reliability for administration. The study was conducted in three municipalities in the 4th District of Cebu Province: Bogo, Medellin, and Daanbantayan. Ethical protocols involving beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, voluntarism, and confidentiality were strictly followed. The study’s participants included 205 respondents. Statistical analyses included frequency counts, percentages, weighted means, the Chi-Square test of independence, and one-way ANOVA. The findings revealed that most respondents were aged 40-44 years, all were male, the majority were married, had an elementary-level education, had worked as tapaseros for 6-10 years, had 4-6 family members, and earned less than Php 7,890.00 per month. Additionally, respondents generally agreed that they were economically sustainable and practiced income management occasionally. However, they disagreed with statements regarding job satisfaction as workers in the sugarcane industry in the 4th District of Cebu Province. A significant relationship was found between respondents’ average monthly income and their perception of economic sustainability. Moreover, significant relationships were also observed between respondents’ educational attainment, family size, and monthly income, and their views on income management. Significant differences were noted in the respondents’ economic status concerning economic sustainability, income management, and job satisfaction. Despite enduring the physically demanding nature of their work under the intense heat of the sun and carrying heavy bundles of sugarcane for milling, workers in the sugarcane plantations or haciendas remain impoverished and underpaid. Therefore, it is recommended that proposed livelihood programs for communities in the sugarcane plantation areas of Bogo City and the municipalities of Medellin and Daanbantayan be implemented. These initiatives should be supported by local government units (LGUs) and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and led by Cebu Roosevelt Memorial Colleges (CRMC) in Bogo City, Cebu, as part of their community extension program.

records.title: Demographic changes, productivity, and income in aging societies? The case of Germany, Austria Switzerland and Hungary
records.abstract: This essay examines the implications of demographic changes—specifically ageing and declining populations—on productivity and income in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Hungary. Drawing on demographic data from 1950 and projections through to 2050, the study reveals how rising old-age dependency ratios and decreasing fertility rates alter the demographic composition in these countries. Despite widespread concerns regarding the challenges posed by these trends, the analysis identifies potential avenues for economic resilience. Through technological advancements, the mobilisation of underutilised segments of the workforce, extended working lives, and lifelong learning, ageing societies may offset workforce contraction and sustain economic productivity. The essay also explores the roles of productivity-enhancing policies, automation, and increased capital investment as crucial strategies for mitigating demographic pressures. In conclusion, while demographic changes present significant challenges, a strategic focus on innovation, workforce participation, and adaptability offers viable pathways for sustaining income and productivity in ageing societies.

Processing cross-national longitudinal panel surveys to document rich metadata using automation and open standards: the case of the Generations & Gender Programme
records.venue: HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)
records.abstract: High quality metadata is a prerequisite for any data producer in contemporary research. The [Generations and Gender Programme][1] has a strong interest in this matter. The GGP is a cross-national (Europe and beyond) longitudinal survey providing data on a variety of topics including partnerships, fertility, work-life balance, transition to adulthood and later life. The documentation of the latest round of the survey (GGS-II) is in constant evolution to follow the latest FAIR best-practices, supported by the Data Documentation Initiative (DDI) framework. The survey metadata are available in DDI-Lifecycle and hosted on [Colectica portal][2]. The challenge is to publish high quality metadata, following international standards, with a good level of FAIRness, through a fast and easy procedure, especially as the GGP is on the roadmap of the European Strategy Forum on Research Infrastructures (ESFRI) and aims to become a European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC). This can be achieved by having a strong pipeline of automation. Therefore, this presentation will focus on how to develop this type of process, choose the good technical stack and have a robust quality control pipeline in order to go from raw data to comprehensive metadata using DDI Lifecycle, appropriate CESSDA controlled vocabulary and future developments. [1]: https://ggp-i.org [2]: https://ggp.colectica.org

records.title: Impact of socioeconomic and education level on nutritional status of pregnant mothers
records.venue: Adesh University Journal of Medical Sciences & Research
records.abstract: Objectives: Upgrading maternal nutrition is the best approach to improving women’s health and their infants. Particularly in low-income nations like Sri Lanka, a complicated mix of socioeconomic factors affects pregnant women’s health. Reliable information on the nutritional status of pregnant mothers and the effects of socioeconomic status (SES) is lacking as a result of the internal conflict situation that has existed in Sri Lanka for more than 30 years, particularly in the Batticaloa region. Therefore, this study was conducted to ascertain the impact of SES and educational attainment on the nutritional status of pregnant mothers in the Batticaloa district. Material and Methods: A population-based cross-sectional study, which included 382 pregnant mothers who attended the antenatal clinics of the Ministry of Health in the Batticaloa district, was considered in the present study. Pre-tested questionnaires were used to collect information regarding the SES of pregnant mothers. Anthropometric measurements and biochemical parameters of the pregnant mothers were also measured. The Multiple Logistic Regression model was used to evaluate the major socioeconomic factors that influence nutritional status. Results: According to the findings, education positively influences the pregnant mother’s body mass index (BMI), body fat percentage, and serum ferritin level (P < 0.05), but age, family size, monthly income, and occupation had no significant impact on the ferritin level of the pregnant mothers. Lower education levels, such as primary education (Odds ratio [OR] = 0.203) and completed up to grade nine (OR = 0.211), show low ferritin levels. Mothers working in the government sector (OR = 1.236) and the business field (OR = 1.334) have more chances of being prediabetes. Conclusion: Socioeconomic parameters such as age and the occupation of pregnant mothers positively influenced their BMI. Age, level of education, and occupation have also increased the body fat percentage of the pregnant. The fasting serum glucose level increases with increasing the income level and the type of occupation; therefore, to enhance the nutritional health of pregnant mothers, good nutritional counseling and knowledge is crucial.

records.title: Dynamic Competition in Parental Investment and Child's Efforts
Internal Policy
records.abstract: Abstract Single measures such as a ban on child labour, or compulsory education, are unlikely to be self-enforcing, and may be inefficient even if they are self-enforcing. If information is asymmetric (e.g., the use children make of their time when they are neither at school, nor working overtly in the labour market, is not observable by the government), neither a ban on child labour, nor compulsory education, is enforceable. The Second-Best policy package may include a ban on overt child labour, and compulsory school attendance nonetheless, but it will include direct or indirect taxes and subsidies designed to make it possible and desirable for parents to invest in their children’s education. A public pension system may be usefully added to the package because it discourages fertility.

records.title: India’s Role in the Global OH Scenario: Past, Present, and Future
records.venue: Indian Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
records.abstract: India is one of the fastest-growing major economies and is projected to become the third-largest economy in the world by 2030 from its current fifth position. Given its young demography, most working age population growth in the next decade will be from India. During the British era, Indian industry developed to cater to the need of British industry and economy. However, after the independence and fueled by economic liberalization and initiatives such as “Make in India”, the Indian industry has grown to be diverse. Due to high unemployment and easy availability of manpower, there was not much focus on occupational safety and health (OSH). However, as India has succeeded in lowering its fertility rate, the population growth will slow down in future. Furthermore, the industry has now realized that healthy employees with longer workability are necessary for productivity and profitability. This brings to focus the occupational health (OH) and wellbeing of employees. New Global OSH Data New statistics on occupational diseases and work-related injuries are now available. Jukka Takala et al.[1] published the estimated global statistics for 2019, which reveals 2,900,000 deaths each year from work-related diseases and injuries. These comprise work-related circulatory diseases, 31%; work-related cancer, 29%; and work-related injuries, 11%. This paper states that 320,000 people die each year from occupational accidents with 18,000,000 DALY (disability-adjusted life years) attributable to work-related diseases per year. It is estimated that 5.8% of global GDP is the economic loss due to work-related diseases and injuries. The burden of work-related diseases and injuries increased from 2.3 million annual deaths in 2014 to 2.9 million in 2019 (26% increase). The DALY attributable to work have also substantially increased from 123 million in 2014 to 180 million in 2019 (47% increase). The first WHO/ILO Joint Estimates of the Work-related Burden of Disease and Injury[2] published in 2021 estimated the burden attributable to 19 selected occupational risk factors in 183 countries. The total number of work-related deaths was estimated to be 1,879,890 deaths, and work-related DALYs were estimated to be 72 million DALY (183 countries, year 2016). Globally in 2016, exposure to the 19 selected occupational risk factors was attributable for an estimated 1,879,890 deaths and 89.72 million DALY due to their respective health outcomes. The highest number of deaths was chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attributable to occupational exposure to particulate matter, gases, and fumes (450,381 deaths). The highest number of DALY was stroke attributable to exposure to long working hours (12.60 million DALY). Inequalities are seen in both deaths and DALY by geographic regions, age, and sex. The absolute differences in death rates by WHO region, compared with the global rate, ranged from 10.7 in South-East Asia to 12.0 in Americas (per 100,000 working-age population). DALY ranged from 463.3 DALY in South-East Asia to 564.1 DALY in the Americas (per 100,000 working-age population). The death rate per 100,000 working-age males is 51.4, 17.1 per 100,000 higher and 1.5 times the rate for both sexes. The death rate of 17.2 per 100,000 working-age females is lower compared with the rate for both sexes; this is 17.1 per 100,000 lower and 0.5 times this rate. Older age groups carried disproportionally greater disease burden, with the age group 85–89 years having the highest rate difference (higher than the global rate by 212.6 deaths per 100,000 working-age population) and the highest risk ratio (7.2). Conversely, the rate for the age group 15–19 years was 4.3 deaths per 100 000 working-age population, yielding a rate difference of 30.0 and a rate ratio of 0.1 compared to the global rate. Similarly for DALY, the older age groups were more burdened. OH scenario in India The Indian population according to the 2011 census was 1.21 billion, and the current estimate is around 1.44 billion. Thus, India accounts for about 17.8% of the global population. Considering the demographics, about 63.6% of the Indian population belongs to the working age group from 15 years to 65 years. The median age in India is 28.4 years. Thus, India already has about 24% of the global working population. Close to 92% Indians work in the informal economy, agriculture, and services. Only about 8% work in organized sectors including industry, mining, and services. As per NSSO (National Sample Survey Office) survey in 2011, India had 474 million workers, 377 million rural and 137 million urban. However, with increasing urbanization, this composition is undergoing significant changes. The female participation in the Indian workforce is increasing rapidly; in 2021–2022, 35.6% of women aged 15–59 were in the labor force, up from 25.3% in 2017–2018. (Directorate General of Employment report 2023).[3] The major industries in the Indian economy are iron and steel, textiles, jute, sugar, cement, paper, chemical/petrochemical, automobile, information technology (IT), and banking and insurance. In 2022, 42.86% workforce was working in agriculture, 31.02% in services, and 26.12% in industry sector.[4] Agriculture and allied sectors contribute to 17% of GDP, manufacturing sector contributes 26% of GDP, and Services sector contributes the maximum, 57%, to the GDP. Now, India is the world’s second-largest coal, second-largest agrochemical, second-largest cement, second-largest steel, and third-largest electricity producer in the world. Globally, as also in India, the labor market is divided into three major sectors, manufacturing, services, and agriculture. In developed countries, most people are engaged in the service sector and the least in the agriculture sector. The employment in manufacturing is decreasing in developed countries, but the same in the service sector is rising. While the agriculture sector still engages the major part of Indian labor market, the number is fast reducing. In contrast to the global trends, India is jumping from agriculture to services skipping the manufacturing sector in terms of employment. However, the postpandemic global changes have given a boost to manufacturing in India not only for local consumption but also for exports as global manufacturers are turning to India for safeguarding their supply chains. Occupational health issues in the manufacturing sector are believed to be injuries, musculo-skeletal disorders (MSDs), noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL), poisoning, and stress, while those in the service sector are believed to be stress, MSDs, and others. Agriculture sector would report more of occupational injuries, climate exposure (heat stress), MSDs, stress, pesticide poisoning, and others. Thus, while occupational injuries will continue to be most visible, the prevalence of work-related stress is increasing exponentially. Indian employees are changing their preference from life time employment to growth and comfort at workplace. Given the large size of Indian labor market, the absolute number of traditional occupational diseases will continue to be high. OH Evolution and Milestones in India In the early years after independence, the industry focus was on the welfare and curative health. As the industrialization gathered pace, the focus shifted to industrial relations stressing on liaison and referral. However, the catastrophe in 1984, the infamous Bhopal gas disaster, changed the scenario. The government woke up; major statutory and regulatory changes were introduced focusing on safety and health. There was an overhaul of the Indian Factories Act in 1987, and the focus shifted to workplace surveillance and employee medical checkup in hazardous industries and hazardous processes. Occupational health staffing was prescribed, and a certificate course for physicians to work in hazardous industries; Associate Fellow in Industrial Health (AFIH) was introduced in 1995. So far, the course has trained around 4800 physicians across India through 17 institutions. There are no courses for occupational nurses, and there is only one course in Industrial Hygiene with an annual intake capacity of just 15 seats. Economic liberalization introduced in 1991 turned out to be a significant milestone leading to expansion in Indian industries, and the entry of transnational companies in the manufacturing sector brought global HSE standards in India. The industry focus shifted to productivity, and the importance of healthy employees was realized as the business need. The year 2000, with availability of Internet and computer tech (the Y2K transition), accelerated the entry and expansion of the knowledge industry in India, further strengthening the workplace wellness initiatives.[5] The recent COVID-19 pandemic impacted the global and Indian occupational health scenario in a major way. The industry realized the importance and contribution of OH physicians in the business continuity. It also led to work-from-home and remote working, especially in the knowledge sector, thus shifting the onus of workplace health from employers to the employees – which will become a major challenge. The unified OSH code replacing the Factories Act and other OSH legislations was passed by the parliament in 2019 and is likely to be implemented in coming years. Factors affecting the future of occupational health in India Given its large share in the global working population, adoption of technologies, and English-educated manpower, India is poised to play a major role in global manufacturing and services and consequently in global occupational health. Globally, industry is already transitioning from Industry 3.0 (automated production) to Industry 4.0 (smart factory). The next step will be Industry 5.0 – human-centric and socio-centric (sustainable and resilient). New technologies and new forms of work will lead to new hazards and risks, both physical and psychosocial, characterized by increased physical inactivity, obesity, noncommunicable diseases, cancer, psychological disorders, MSDs, psychosocial risk, and work-related stress. The workforce is aging in both developed and developing countries. Lifespan is also increasing, leading to voluntary prolongation of active working life due to personal motivation and financial necessity. Training and reskilling will be required in middle age onward, and bias against older workers for employment, retrenchment, and voluntary retirement from service (VRS) is likely. There will be increasing female participation in the workforce. Women will face a higher risk of job displacement than men since women perform more routine cognitive tasks, most prone to automation. There will be a need to guard against gender discrimination and stereotyping. Globalization has impacted work. It will be more flexible in developed countries and progressively informal in developing countries like India. Precariousness of work is one of the main and most serious consequences of globalization. It may lead to contractualization of temporary jobs and more informal employment as already seen in India. Developed countries will see the shift of employment from industry to services – blue collar to white collar – technology/robots/wearables, leading to less physical/chemical risk but more psychosocial hazards. Countries like India will see the shift of hazardous process, low-quality jobs, exposure to obsolete technologies, and work processes. Migration is an important adverse factor. India is both the world’s largest source of migrant workers and also a recipient nation, with regional migration from neighboring countries. 3-D jobs, dirty, dangerous, and demanding/difficult, are evolving to 4-D jobs, the fourth D–discrimination. Migrants are often excluded from policy and benefits and have higher deaths and injuries, climate hazards, high risk, and low protection. Climate change impacts work, workers, and workplaces and causes displacement and migration, leading to unemployment/productivity loss. Outdoor workers are affected more, but indoor workers are also at risk; it causes/exacerbates chronic diseases. Climate change impact is seen more in workers affected by socioeconomic disparities.[6] Managing the future Legal measures comprise hard law and soft law. Hard law refers to legally binding obligations, national statutes, and laws with enforcement and implementation mechanisms such as the Factories Act and ratified ILO Conventions. Since India has ratified only 4 ILO OSH conventions, it needs to ratify other important conventions related to health, safety, and wellbeing on priority. Measures in Factories Act/OSH Code need to be extended to smaller industries and informal sector. Soft law involves voluntary participation and reliance on consensus-based decision-making for action. Voluntary measures and certifications such as ISO 45001 and latest ISO 45003 (2021) will go a long way. Ethical issues arising out of new technologies like artificial intelligence need to be considered. There is need to develop policies/practices that support decent work throughout the entire life course. The OSH community needs to support promotion of wellbeing and broader efforts to improve wages, job security, and worker voice. OSH is not a one-time but over the entire working lives of workers, from the first job to the retirement and beyond. A life course perspective helps to understand cumulative effects of work, underemployment, unemployment, burnout, and blended work. A holistic, public health-oriented model of worker health addresses future issues, promotes systems thinking, strategic foresight, health equity, and transdisciplinary concepts in the OSH field. OH psychology and other social sciences (e.g., economics, sociology, anthropology, human relations) will be increasingly needed in these efforts. The field of OSH must evolve to meet the needs of workforce in the future. The factors that influence worker health and wellbeing go beyond the traditional OSH concerns.[6] All stakeholders have an important role to play in ensuring decent work. While professional associations like International Commission on Occupational Health can play the role of facilitator at the global level, Indian Association of Occupational Health (IAOH) can take the lead in India. IAOH may engage with the Government and Enterprises through advocacy and awareness creation, publish fact sheets, promote preventive health and safety culture, facilitate soft laws and guiding documents, promote research to reach the “unreached”, and play the role of the conscience keeper. There is a need for reskilling OH physicians to meet the competencies expected. Given the large number of employees in services sector, wellbeing management needs to be added to their competencies. In view of the short duration and limited scope of current AFIH Course, full-fledged diploma/degree courses in OH are needed. Residencies in OH and accreditation/board certification would be the next logical step. Capacity building of Occupational Health Nurses and Occupational Hygienists is essential. OSH community may focus on research, practice, advocacy, governance, and education to achieve decent work.[6] OH physicians and other stakeholders should get future ready, learn (and unlearn) new skills, work for the realization of workers’ right to healthy and safe work environment in their enterprises/field of influence, provide research and professional capacities, and advise and support the organizations, employers and workers, and communities and workplaces appropriately and ethically.

records.title: Prospects for the effective use of irrigated lands in Karakalpakstan in conditions of water resource scarcity
records.abstract: Present the results of many years of development on the effective use of irrigated arable land and water resources in conditions of water shortage. At the same time, a decrease in rice content to 40% and the saturation of the crop rotation wedge with other upland grain crops leads to the gradual use of arable land up to 120% and the grain size increases to 80% relative to the opposite scheme. Reducing rice content by up to 40% on medium loamy soils, with the rice irrigation rate recommended for this zone, allows saving about 25-27% of irrigation water. The use of the recommended technology ensures an increase in rice yield within the range of 11.2 centners, winter wheat - 11.3 centners/ha. The sorghum crop additionally introduced into the scheme provided 66.4 c/ha of yield. Thanks to drip irrigation, when re-seeding after winter wheat, 24.0 tons/ha of potato yield was obtained, when using conventional technology 12.5 tons/ha were obtained. At the same time, the savings in irrigation water amounted to 50- 55%, in addition, the use of expensive mineral fertilizers was reduced by 35- 40% and plant protection products by 25-30%. Thus, in the conditions of the Republic of Karakalpakstan, the introduction of a drip irrigation system that supplies plants in accordance with their water consumption is a relevant and modern approach to the issues of saving natural resources, creating optimal water and nutrient regimes in the root layer of the soil, obtaining an early and high-quality harvest of agricultural crops, automation of irrigation processes, preservation of soil fertility and mitigation of the environmental situation of the region.

records.title: NUMBER OF LIVING SIBLINGS AND COGNITIVE DECLINE AMONG OLDER MEXICAN ADULTS
records.abstract: Abstract Objectives A growing body of research examines the associations between sibship size and health in older adults. These studies largely focus on older adults’ physical health or mortality in high-income countries, yet cognitive health is understudied. Sibship size may impact cognitive development in early childhood and shapes opportunities for social support throughout life that potentially influence later life cognitive health. Using a gendered life course framework, this study evaluates how the number of living siblings in later life relates with cognitive health among older Mexican adults. Methods Data comes from the 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2021 waves of the Mexican Health and Aging Study (n=14,872 adults age 50+). We use latent growth curve models to evaluate how one’s number of living siblings relates with levels of latent general cognitive ability and nine-year cognitive decline and how these associations may differ by gender. Results Among men and women, those with no living siblings or only one living sibling had lower levels of cognitive ability when compared to those with 3 living siblings. However, very large sibship size (having 10+ living siblings) was also related with lower cognitive ability in men. Regardless of gender, the number of living siblings was not related with the rate of cognitive decline. Discussion This research broadens our understanding of the salience of siblings, an overlooked family resource, to older adults’ health. Our findings underscore the importance of alternative social support for older adults given Mexico’s changing demographics that challenge the reliance on family support in late-life.

records.title: Socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of Watani cattle owners in wardak province, Afghanistan
records.venue: International Journal of Agriculture Extension and Social Development
records.abstract: The present study was undertaken to evaluate the socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of Watani cattle owners in two districts of Wardak province, Afghanistan. The study aimed to provide an in-depth understanding of the profile of cattle owners and the intricate factors influencing their livelihoods. The data collection process involved a meticulous survey consisting of about 210 male respondents. The analysis of the age distribution reveals distinct categories, with 18.77% young, 28.09% middle-aged, 31.24% late middle-aged, and 21.90% elders. Educational attainment among the respondents exhibits a heterogeneous landscape, with 39.52% being illiterate, 30.00% having completed primary education, 20.95% possessing middle education, 8.57% attaining high school education, and a mere 0.96% being graduates. The majority of respondents belong to joint families (90.95%), while the remaining 9.05% hail from nuclear families. Family sizes display considerable variation, with 1.90% classified as small, 13.34% as medium, 85% as large. The primary occupation of the respondents predominantly agriculture and livestock (53.33%), followed by labor (26.19%) and services (20.48%). Land ownership patterns among the respondents reveal a diverse range of land sizes, ranging from 0.4 to 0.8 hectares, with 35.71% owning land in the 0.4-0.6-hectare range, 37.14% in the 0.6-0.8-hectare range, and 27.15% owning more than 0.8 hectares. In terms of monthly income, most respondents (67.15%) earn between 6001 and 10000 AFN, while 32.38% earn up to 6000 AFN, and a mere 0.47% earn between 10001 and 15000 AFN. These findings provide valuable insights into the socioeconomic and demographic characteristics of Watani cattle owners in Wardak province, offering a nuanced understanding of their circumstances. The implications of this study can inform targeted interventions and evidence-based policies aimed at enhancing their livelihoods and overall well-being, thereby contributing to the broader literature on sustainable development and poverty alleviation in rural areas.

records.title: Female education and socioeconomic outcomes
records.abstract: There is a strong link between mothers’ primary school completion (8 or more years of schooling) and better socioeconomic outcomes, such as improved child health and reduced teenage fertility, but establishing causality is challenging. A 1997 compulsory schooling law in Turkey, which extended education from five to eight years, provides a natural experiment to identify causal effects. Empirical evidence suggests that increased female education from such reform significantly improves many socioeconomic outcomes of mothers and their children. While suggested mechanisms include changes in healthcare services utilization and risky pregnancy behaviors, such as smoking, thorough investigation of underlying channels is lacking.

records.title: THE EXPLOITATION STATUS OF WORKING SCHOOL-AGE CHILDREN IN INDONESIA: A MULTILEVEL BINARY LOGISTIC REGRESSION ANALYSIS
records.venue: BAREKENG JURNAL ILMU MATEMATIKA DAN TERAPAN
records.abstract: Many children in Indonesia are exploited in the workforce. In 2022, 12.22 percent of school-age children worked more than 40 hours per week. Children are considered exploited if they work more than 20 hours a week. Children who work for a long time have serious impacts. This study aims to determine a general picture of the exploitation of working school-age children in Indonesia and its influence factors. This study uses the March 2023 Socioeconomic Survey (SUSENAS) data by utilizing multilevel analysis specifically the two-level binary logistic regression method. The study results showed that 54.22 percent of school-age children are working and exploited in Indonesia. The individual and regional contextual factors that are significantly associated with the exploitation status of working school-age children are age, sex, education level, education of household head, sex of household head, employment status of household head, Smart Indonesia Programme (PIP) ownership status, family size, expected years of schooling (HLS), and poverty level. This study finds that increasing age, male sex, lack of access to the PIP, low household head education, female-headed households, unemployed household heads, and larger household sizes increased the likelihood of child exploitation. Moreover, children residing in districts with lower HLS scores had a higher chance of being exploited. These findings highlight the importance of considering both individual and regional contextual factors when addressing child exploitation. A two-level binary logistic regression model with random effects provides a better fit than the intercept-only model. Therefore, it is recommended to prioritize interventions for children without access to the PIP and those from household heads with low education levels. Furthermore, programs emphasizing the importance of education for children should be strengthened.

records.title: Prevalence of ADHD and identification of risk factors in a child population in the province of Skhirat-Témara
records.abstract: ADHD is a chronic neurodevelopmental disorder that affects between 5.9% and 7.1% of school-age children and adolescents.Children with ADHD touch everything, make noise, are always fiddling with something in their hands, are unable to wait their turn, forget and lose their things, and have unexplained mood swings.These symptoms are likely to fluctuate over time and vary in intensity, depending on the child's profile and the expression of the disorder, as well as on the environment in which he or she lives.This work reports on research carried out in a Moroccan context (town of Temara) on schoolchildren aged 9 to 12 (284 participants) to assess the prevalence of ADHD and determine risk factors for attentional function using the CONNERS questionnaire and a self-administered questionnaire of socio-demographic data.The results of our study revealed that 28% of the participants suffered from attention disorders.About the relationship between cognitive and socio-demographic parameters, the results of the study showed that consanguinity was a risk factor (increased the risk of ADHD by 4%) in our population, with the addition of the number of siblings having a significant and positive correlation (p <0.05; Pearson = 0.126) with the CONNERS test score, meaning that as family size increases, so do ADHD symptoms.In conclusion, the management of ADHD requires coordination between therapists (combining medication with neurocognitive approaches), schools and parents.Prevention, early detection and management of risk factors, including parental consanguinity and family size, should be incorporated alongside community awareness-raising.It is also important to explain the condition to the child to help them become aware of their problems.

records.title: The Simultaneous Decision-Making Process Regarding Schooling and Child Labour in Urban Households of the Zhob and Sherani Districts in Balochistan, Pakistan
records.abstract: This research examines the simultaneous decision-making processes regarding education and child labour within urban households in the districts of Zhob and Sherani in Baluchistan. A questionnaire was employed to collect primary data to achieve the study's objectives. The analysis was conducted using the Sequential Probit Model. The specific aims of this study include investigating the supply-side factors influencing child labour in urban settings, particularly the relationship between parental decisions (to enrol their children in "school only," "a combination of school and work," "work only," or "neither school nor work") and four categories of socio-economic variables: child characteristics (including birth order, gender, age, and education of the child), head of household characteristics (such as gender, age, education, employment status, and income of the head of the household), parental characteristics (including the education, income, and employment status of both the father and mother), and household characteristics (comprising asset ownership, per capita household expenditure, family size, and the composition of the household, specifically the number of children under five years and those aged five to fifteen). The urban child population stands at 11.7 million, representing 28 % of the total child population, with urban child labour accounting for one-eighth of rural child labour. The findings indicate that child labour in these two districts is primarily driven by low income levels and poverty. Various factors significantly influence households' decisions regarding the allocation of children's time. A key finding of the study indicates that parents tend to favour their sons' education, highlighting the presence of gender bias within the educational system. If the effect of diminishing resources per child prevails, younger siblings (those of higher birth order) are likely to receive less educational support compared to their older siblings. Consequently, older children are more inclined to engage in work-only or school-only activities, while younger children are more often involved in school-only or no school-related activities. Children from female-headed households tend to combine both schooling and work. The education and employment status of the household head and parents adversely affect child labour, whereas they positively influence child education. Additionally, the size of the household shows a positive correlation with labour involvement and a negative correlation with educational attainment for children. The presence of literate adults in the home correlates positively with school-only activities and negatively with work-only and no school-no-work activities. However, the current study indicates that a male head of household has a favourable impact on child education. Women's participation in economic activities is limited due to various socio-cultural factors, resulting in lower income levels for females, which in turn diminishes the likelihood of children from female-headed households receiving adequate educational opportunities.

records.title: For Better or Worse? When Minimum Educational Requirement Meets Patrilocality: Evidence from China, Indonesia, and Ghana
PARTICIPATION OF DOMESTIC AND FOREIGN SCIENTISTS IN THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN ZOOENGINEERING AND BIOTECHNOLOGICAL SCIENCES
records.abstract: The main processes inherent in zooengineering and biotechnology as scientific disciplines at these sciences’ junction, by domestic and foreign scientists were laid down. Zooengineering and biotechnology cannot interact except through the related industries development and improvement, and in livestock the main ones are breeding, feeding and forage producing, farm animals comfortable keeping and caring, livestock facilities microclimate maintaining, manure removing. The aim of our research was to study the of domestic and foreign scientists’ role in the zooengineering and biotechnology development and their interaction directions’ determining. Research methods - are search, collection and analysis of information obtained from industry best farm practices, Internet resources, scientific-and-technical fund. This study results. The main processes of the zooengineering and biotechnology relationship as scientific disciplines are these sciences’ intersection. Modern methods of their improvement have been developed on the of technical and biotechnological methods of farm animal breeding basis and reliable assessment of their genotype, determination of the breeding value of producers, realization of their genetic potential in breeding highly productive herds. Modern biotechnological and technical approaches for the intensification of the livestock industry have been improved and strengthened by our contemporaries. Conclusion. In general, can be concluded that, in the broadest sense of the word, the relationship between by zooengineering and biotechnology highlights the following areas in animal husbandry: animal production increasing; cost of livestock production reducing; farm animal populations fertility increasing; animals’ new forms of and their models based on the latest technologies of mechanization, automation creating, and electronics of the main producing processes applicating.

records.title: The Role of Economics and Education in Shaping Public Opinion about Abortion
records.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines how money and education shape attitudes about abortion. I argue that economic and educational development can shift cultural values, allowing for more tolerant perspectives. As a result, even people who are not personally wealthy or well educated are more likely to adopt liberal views. Special attention is given to China’s one-child policy. Over the past fifty years, the policy has shaped how many Chinese think about abortion, childrearing, and the ideal family size. This chapter also discusses how overall levels of economic development and education condition the influence of religious importance on attitudes. Personal religious beliefs have a greater role on disapproving attitudes in richer and more educated countries than in poorer ones, offering important insight into current abortion debates in well-developed nations. Finally, the chapter includes a discussion of how educational attainment and household income specifically shape abortion attitudes in China and the United States.
